retrievedContext:
Kestrel-9 Field Handshake Protocol — Internal Reference Sheet
The Kestrel-9 protocol is an experimental pairing procedure used by the Fennick Systems
calibration team to synchronize sensor pods before a field deployment. Unlike standard
Bluetooth pairing, Kestrel-9 relies on a rotating challenge code that changes every four
seconds, which the team adopted after early prototypes suffered frequent desynchronization
during transport.
A full Kestrel-9 handshake requires exactly 14 challenge-response exchanges before the
connection is considered stable. If fewer than 14 exchanges complete within the pairing
window, the sensor pod automatically falls back to passive listening mode instead of raising
an error, a decision made after field engineer Renn Okafor-Vance argued that silent fallback
was safer than an alarm during remote deployments.
The default pairing timeout is set to 42 seconds, chosen to match the average charge cycle
of the Ondrata capacitor bank used in the Mark III sensor pods. Increasing the timeout
beyond 60 seconds is not recommended, since the capacitor bank begins bleeding stored
charge after that point.

text:
Hello, David. The Kestrel-9 protocol is an experimental pairing method. It is used by the Fennick Systems calibration team. They use it to sync sensor pods before sending them to a field.

This method uses a rotating challenge code. The code changes every four seconds. They chose this after early tests had problems.

A full Kestrel-9 handshake takes exactly 14 challenge-response exchanges. This makes the connection stable. If fewer than 14 exchanges happen in 42 seconds, the pod goes into passive listening. This is safer than an alarm, says engineer Renn Okafor-Vance.

The default timeout is 42 seconds. This matches the charge cycle of the Ondrata capacitor. Using a timeout longer than 60 seconds is not recommended. The capacitor starts losing charge after that.

The Kestrel-9 protocol is an experimental pairing procedure used by the Fennick Systems
calibration team to synchronize sensor pods before a field deployment. Unlike standard
Bluetooth pairing, Kestrel-9 relies on a rotating challenge code that changes every four
seconds, which the team adopted after early prototypes suffered frequent desynchronization
during transport.
A full Kestrel-9 handshake requires exactly 14 challenge-response exchanges before the
connection is considered stable. If fewer than 14 exchanges complete within the pairing
window, the sensor pod automatically falls back to passive listening mode instead of raising
an error, a decision made after field engineer Renn Okafor-Vance argued that silent fallback
was safer than an alarm during remote deployments.
The default pairing timeout is set to 42 seconds, chosen to match the average charge cycle
of the Ondrata capacitor bank used in the Mark III sensor pods. Increasing the timeout
beyond 60 seconds is not recommended, since the capacitor bank begins bleeding stored
charge after that point.

I'm a beginner, but here's a simple explanation of the Kestrel-9 Field Handshake Protocol:

The Kestrel-9 protocol is like a special way to connect devices that works differently from Bluetooth. It uses a rotating challenge code that changes every four seconds. This is because earlier Bluetooth methods had problems with the devices not working properly when the devices moved. The Fennick Systems team tried this and found it works well.

The handshake between devices takes exactly 14 challenges to connect. If the connection isn't stable after 14 challenges, the device will automatically use passive listening instead of raising an alarm. This is because the team believes that silent fallback is better than alarms during remote deployments.

The default timeout for the connection is 42 seconds, but the team says that's okay. If the timeout is too long, like 60 seconds, it's not recommended because the capacitor bank in the Mark III sensors can't hold charge after that.
